answer_text:
We need a generator \(\alpha\) of the ideal

\[
(3+5i,\;1+3i)\subseteq \mathbb{Z}[i].
\]

Since \(\mathbb{Z}[i]\) is a Euclidean domain, this ideal is generated by a greatest common divisor of \(3+5i\) and \(1+3i\), up to multiplication by a unit.

Apply the Euclidean algorithm.

First divide \(3+5i\) by \(1+3i\):

\[
\frac{3+5i}{1+3i}
= \frac{(3+5i)(1-3i)}{10}
= \frac{18-4i}{10}
= 1.8-0.4i.
\]

A nearby Gaussian integer is \(2\). Thus

\[
3+5i = 2(1+3i) + (1-i).
\]

So

\[
(3+5i,\;1+3i) = (1+3i,\;1-i).
\]

Now divide \(1+3i\) by \(1-i\):

\[
\frac{1+3i}{1-i}
= \frac{(1+3i)(1+i)}{2}
= \frac{-2+4i}{2}
= -1+2i.
\]

This division is exact, so

\[
1+3i = (-1+2i)(1-i).
\]

Hence \(1-i\) divides both \(1+3i\) and \(3+5i\). Also, from

\[
3+5i = 2(1+3i)+(1-i),
\]

we see that \(1-i\) belongs to the ideal \((3+5i,1+3i)\).

Therefore,

\[
(3+5i,\;1+3i) = (1-i).
\]

Thus one valid choice is

\[
\boxed{1-i}.
\]

Any unit multiple of \(1-i\) would also work.
